# Lead-Time Compression Without Quality Compromise
## An Operations Plan for a Certified Industrial Equipment Manufacturer

---

## 1. The Reframe (read this first)

Three things are almost certainly true, and all three change the shape of the answer:

**1. The competitor is not building faster. They are quoting from a different starting point.** A 6-week promise on certified industrial equipment is not achievable by working harder inside a 14-week process. It is achievable by holding standard modules in stock, restricting the configuration space, and beginning the clock after the long-lead content is already on the shelf. The gap is **offer architecture**, not shop-floor speed. You cannot close it with a factory program alone.

**2. Almost none of the 14 weeks is work.** In engineered industrial equipment, value-added touch time is typically 8–15% of quoted lead time. The rest is queue, kit shortages, batch waiting, inspector availability, document assembly, engineering rework and — critically — **embedded safety padding** that planning added because the promise was unreliable. You are not fighting a capacity problem. You are fighting a waiting problem plus a promising problem.

**3. The last compression attempt failed for a reason that is diagnosable, and it was not "inspections take too long."** Warranty spikes after schedule compression have a standard signature: work released without complete kits, assembly performed out of sequence, parts substituted under deviation, rework absorbed informally, overtime fatigue, and documentation dossiers back-filled at the end rather than captured at the gate. **The gates did not fail. The discipline around the gates failed under expediting pressure.** That distinction is the entire foundation of this plan — and the only basis on which Quality will cooperate.

**The organising principle:** *gate **integrity** is untouchable; gate **logistics** are fully in scope.*

| Untouchable (change requires MRB / notified-body approval) | Fully in scope |
|---|---|
| Inspection content, acceptance criteria, sampling plans | Who performs the inspection (certified operator vs. inspector) |
| Witness and hold points, NDT scope | When inspectors are staffed and scheduled |
| Documentation completeness at ship | Where inspection happens (in-line vs. remote lab) |
| Certification and traceability requirements | Recording medium (born-digital vs. paper, back-filled) |
| | Fixtures, gauges, tooling duplication |
| | Sequence and overlap of non-dependent gates |

---

## 2. Diagnosis: Where the Time Actually Goes

### 2.1 The 30-day time ledger (do this before anything else)

Take the last 120 shipped orders. Reconstruct a time-stamped ledger from **customer inquiry to customer receipt** — not from order release, which is where most manufacturers start measuring and thereby hide 20% of the lead time. For every order, split each stage into **touch time** and **wait time**.

Illustrative result for a 14-week (70 working-day) quote:

| Stage | Elapsed | Touch | Wait / cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inquiry → order entry (config validation, credit, spec clarification) | 8 d | 1 d | Sequential handoffs; sales-engineering ping-pong |
| Engineering release / drawing approval | 9 d | 2 d | One-off specials; no reuse library; customer approval loop |
| Purchased long-lead content (castings, drives, certified components) | 25 d | — | **Order-triggered** procurement; no capacity reserved |
| Kit staging | 5 d | 1 d | 2–3 shortages per order; partial-kit releases |
| Fabrication / machining | 12 d | 3 d | Batch campaigns; queue before the constraint |
| Assembly | 7 d | 3 d | Out-of-sequence work; waiting on missing items |
| In-process certified inspections | 7 d | **1.2 d** | **Inspector availability, not inspection** |
| Final test + certification dossier | 8 d | 2 d | Documents assembled retroactively; NDT subcontract turnaround |
| Pack / ship consolidation | 4 d | 1 d | Weekly truck consolidation |
| **Planning safety padding embedded in the quote** | **~10 d** | — | Compensation for unreliable promise |
| **Total (with overlaps)** | **70 d** | **~14 d (20%)** | **~56 d** |

### 2.2 The five real thieves

| # | Thief | Typical share of the gap | Why it persists |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Order-triggered procurement of long-lead items** | Largest single block | Nobody owns pre-commitment risk; finance resists inventory |
| 2 | **Decoupling point too far upstream** — everything is made-to-order from raw | Structural | Product was never modularised; configuration space unbounded |
| 3 | **Inspector as an unmanaged constraint** — 6:1 queue-to-touch ratio | 5–7 days | Quality headcount cut as "overhead"; not scheduled as capacity |
| 4 | **Partial-kit release and WIP overload** | 8–12 days *and* the warranty risk | Releasing early *feels* fast; it is the root cause of out-of-sequence work |
| 5 | **Padding to cover unreliability** | ~10 days | Rational planning behaviour; only removable by proving reliability |

### 2.3 Two facts to verify, not assume

- **Test the "one in three on delivery speed" claim.** Run a structured win/loss audit on 40 lost deals with the *customer*, not the salesperson. Delivery is the most socially acceptable reason a buyer gives for a price-driven loss. Expect the true figure to be 15–25% — still a large prize, but it changes the investment case.
- **Test whether the problem is length or reliability.** If you quote 14 weeks and deliver in 17, buyers discount your promise and buy from the firm that hits its date. Measure OTD to *original* promise date. If it is below 80%, **reliability must be fixed before the quote is shortened** — otherwise you have simply moved the lie forward.

---

## 3. The Plan: Five Levers

### Lever 1 — Offer architecture (the biggest single win, and it is commercial)

You cannot quote 6 weeks on everything. You can quote 6 weeks on the 50–60% of volume where you actually lose the deals.

**Tiered quote menu, published and enforced:**

| Tier | Content | Volume | Quoted lead time | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Express** | Pre-defined configurations from stocked modules; no drawing approval | 50–55% | **5–6 weeks** | List |
| **Standard** | Catalogue options within the rules engine | 30–35% | 8–9 weeks | List −0/+2% |
| **Engineered** | True custom / new engineering | 10–15% | 14–16 weeks | Premium, priced for it |

Supporting moves: a **configuration rules engine (CPQ)** that auto-generates BOM and routing for Tiers 1–2 with no engineering touch; a **design freeze rule** (spec changes after Day 5 reset the clock and re-price); a **specials tariff** so one-off engineering is a priced choice rather than a free default; and **capacity slot reservation** — sales can book a production slot at quote stage, which converts the quote from a forecast into a commitment.

**Guardrail:** cap Express at a defined share of monthly slots and attach an expedite tariff with a hard fence. Otherwise sales will sell only the fastest tier at the lowest price and you will have moved the bottleneck, not removed it.

### Lever 2 — Supply (attack the 25-day block)

| Action | Mechanism | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Identify the 12–20 items on the critical path | Lead-time × criticality Pareto | Focus |
| **Capacity reservation agreements** | Pay for reserved supplier capacity + rolling 6-month forecast; call off against it | Converts 8-week procurement into 1-week call-off |
| **Consignment / VMI** on 8–10 certified components | Supplier owns stock at your dock | Removes procurement from the critical path entirely |
| **Delegated source inspection** | Certify supplier QA to perform and document release inspection; you audit | Eliminates incoming-inspection queue **without weakening the gate** |
| **Dual-source** the two most fragile items | Qualification program (6–9 months) | Removes single-point schedule risk |
| **Retainer with notified body / NDT provider** | Guaranteed inspector availability windows | Removes 3–5 days of third-party queue |

### Lever 3 — Inventory (buffer deliberately, in one place)

Do **not** raise raw material broadly. Place inventory at exactly one place: the **decoupling point**.

- Stock **6–8 base modules / semi-finished assemblies** covering the Express configurations, sized by demand variability × replenishment lead time, replenished by kanban on a level schedule.
- Hold **consignment stock** on the critical purchased items (Lever 2).
- Introduce **postponement**: perform variant-creating operations (final machining, controls configuration, paint, labelling, documentation) as the last steps, not the first.
- Estimated working capital: **$7–10M one-time**, against which set the release from lower WIP (WIP falls with the cap in Lever 4) and reduced expedite freight.

### Lever 4 — Flow and scheduling (the cheapest and fastest lever)

| Rule | Detail | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **No release without a complete kit** | 100% kit verification before order release; shortages held at the gate, not on the floor | This single rule is the primary defence against the out-of-sequence work that caused the warranty spike |
| **WIP cap (CONWIP)** | Hard cap on orders on the floor; new order releases only on completion | Halves queue time with zero capital. Little's Law, not opinion |
| **Drum-buffer-rope on the true constraint** | Identify the constraint (frequently inspection, not machining); protect it with a time buffer; schedule everything else to it | Stops local optimisation |
| **Level-load, break batch campaigns** | Smaller, more frequent runs; invest in setup reduction / duplicate fixtures | Batching is a hidden 4–6 days |
| **Daily shortage and hold escalation** | Tiered daily management: cell → value stream → plant, 15 minutes each | Makes waiting visible within 24 hours |
| **Single-piece flow of documentation** | Certification dossier built at each gate, digitally, in real time | Removes 4–6 days of end-of-line document assembly *and* eliminates back-filling |

### Lever 5 — Quality gate throughput (the counter-intuitive lever)

Every gate stays. You attack the queue in front of it.

1. **Add inspection capacity.** 2–4 additional certified inspectors, plus shift coverage aligned to when work actually arrives at gates. Cost ~$0.5–0.8M/yr; typical saving 5–7 days of lead time. This is usually the highest-ROI item in the entire plan, and it is a reversal of the cost logic that created the problem.
2. **Schedule inspection as capacity, not as an event.** Inspectors appear on the production schedule with committed windows and a published **SLA: gate response within 4 hours of readiness call**. This is Quality's side of the bargain — and it is what makes them a partner rather than a bottleneck.
3. **Delegated in-process verification.** Certify and qualify operators to perform defined in-process checks under a documented training/qualification matrix, with inspector audit sampling and full traceability. Approved through MRB and, where applicable, the notified body — *in advance*, in writing.
4. **Move inspection to the work.** Portable gauges, in-cell measurement, in-line NDT capacity rather than transporting parts to a central lab.
5. **Attack defects to attack time.** Rework loops are the largest hidden lead-time component in certified equipment. Drive first-pass yield with poka-yoke, fixtures, work instructions and root-cause closure. **Every point of FPY improvement buys lead time and reduces warranty simultaneously** — this is the argument that converts Quality from obstacle to sponsor.
